sections.h2: Which sale routes suit a Chicago owner who wants speed?
sections.html:
Chicago owners can go through a broker, handle the sale personally, or take a purchase offer from a buyer who pays cash. Each trades time, price and effort differently, and the right pick turns on the building's condition and how soon you need to close.

  • Broker listing. Photos, showings and an open house period come first, followed by a buyer who usually needs a mortgage and an appraisal. Problems found in the buyer's inspection get renegotiated.
  • Sale by owner. You skip the agent fee but take on pricing, showings, the contract and the disclosure paperwork. An Illinois real estate attorney normally reviews the contract.
  • Cash purchase. The buyer takes the building in its present state, so repairs, staging and lender timelines drop out. Offers usually come in below a fully prepared retail sale, so weigh the figure against what you would net after fixing the building, carrying it and paying fees.

All three routes share the same public steps: a transfer tax declaration, a deed recorded in Cook County and a seller disclosure report.

sections.h2: What does Chicago look like in the Census numbers?
sections.html:
Chicago is a very large city made of many separate housing markets, so a street-by-street view matters more than the citywide average. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 2,731,585 residents across 227.73 square miles of land, a density of about 12,060 per square mile in the 2020 count.

Chicago received its city charter on March 4, 1837 and rebuilt after the fire of October 8, 1871, which burned an area about four miles long and a mile wide. It sits on the southwestern shore of Lake Michigan and is the seat of Cook County. University of Chicago sociologists divided it into community areas in the late 1920s, and the city now recognizes 77 of them, containing more than 200 informal neighborhoods.

The 2020 to 2024 Census housing figures show how mixed the stock is. Just 46.0 percent of Chicago households own the home they live in, owner-occupied homes carry a median value of $334,100, and typical gross rent is $1,440 a month. There are 1,160,205 households averaging 2.29 people.

sections.h2: How much transfer tax does a Chicago sale carry?
sections.html:
Three layers of transfer tax can apply to a Chicago sale: a state tax, a city tax and a surcharge for the Chicago Transit Authority. At the state level, Section 31-10 of the Property Tax Code taxes a transfer at fifty cents per $500 of the value stated in the declaration, or fraction of $500.

The City of Chicago adds its own real property transfer tax. Its Department of Finance prints the rate as $5.25 per $500 of transfer price, made up of a $3.75 city portion and a $1.50 CTA portion. In general the buyer owes the $3.75 and the seller owes the $1.50. Section 3-33-060 of the municipal code lists the exemptions, and the page says none applies unless the declaration describes supporting facts and attaches documents.

Where each piece of Chicago transfer paperwork goes
ItemWhere it is handledSource
Transfer tax declarationFiled online through MyDec; the city does not take declarations by mailChicago Department of Finance
Transfer stampsDepartment of Finance counter at 121 N. LaSalle, Room 107, or a registered title companyChicago Department of Finance
Deed recordingCook County Clerk, Recordings DivisionCook County Clerk
State transfer taxFifty cents per $500 of declared valueReal Estate Transfer Tax Law, Article 31

One break is worth knowing about. The city page describes a refund of the CTA portion for a buyer who is at least 65, lives in the home for a year or more and paid $250,000 or less. Have the title company confirm which lines apply to your contract, since the buyer and seller can agree to split charges differently.

sections.h2: Who records a Chicago deed, and what happens at the filing?
sections.html:
The Cook County Clerk's Recordings Division records Chicago deeds, and the city itself does not. The office keeps land records and lets anyone search them by property index number, grantor, grantee and other indexed details.

Hours run from nine to five, and the office says its last customer is accepted at 4:45 pm. Its site also carries a Property Fraud Unit for owners who find a suspicious filing against their home and a legal help desk where a volunteer attorney can answer recording questions.

In a typical closing the title company or attorney prepares the declaration, buys the stamps and sends the deed for filing, so most sellers never visit a counter.

sections.h2: Which Cook County tax exemptions affect a Chicago house?
sections.html:
The Assessor's exemptions decide how much of a Chicago home's assessed value gets taxed, and a missing one is a common reason a bill runs high. The Homeowner Exemption lowers equalized assessed value by $10,000, renews automatically once granted, and the Assessor says it saves the average Cook County owner roughly $950 a year.

  • Senior Exemption: for owner-occupants 65 or older, renewed automatically.
  • Senior Freeze: household income at or under $65,000 for calendar year 2024, and it has to be filed every year.
  • Long-Time Homeowner Exemption: the Assessor says only about 2 percent of homeowners qualify, and applications are mailed to those who may be eligible.
  • Home Improvement Exemption: applied automatically, shielding up to $75,000 of added value for four years at most.

Exemptions show up as deductions on the second installment bill. When one was left off, a Certificate of Error can recover the savings for tax years 2021 through 2025. Second installment bills for 2025 were mailed September 1, 2026 and fell due October 1, 2026. Tell your closing agent about any pending Certificate of Error.

sections.h2: What must a Chicago seller disclose under Illinois law?
sections.html:
Illinois requires a seller of residential property to fill out a written disclosure report and deliver it to the buyer ahead of signing. That duty sits in Section 20 of the Residential Real Property Disclosure Act, and Section 35 prints the form.

The form poses yes, no or not applicable questions about conditions the seller actually knows of. Several bear on older Chicago buildings: flooding or recurring leakage in a basement or crawl space, defects in the foundation, roof, electrical and plumbing systems, unsafe radon or asbestos, and lead paint or lead water and plumbing pipes. It also asks about termites, underground fuel tanks, boundary disputes and uncorrected violation notices.

The form states that the parties may still agree to an as-is sale, and the seller keeps a continuing duty to update the report before closing. It also warns that completing it creates legal obligations for the seller.

sections.h2: How do Chicago winters and older buildings affect a quick sale?
sections.html:
Chicago has a humid continental climate with hot summers and four distinct seasons. Winters bring cold and snow, the normal high from December through March is about 36 degrees Fahrenheit, and measurable snow can continue into the first or second week of April. Summer heat waves are frequent, though lake breezes keep the shoreline cooler.

Lake Michigan moderates temperatures, so waterfront neighborhoods run slightly warmer in winter and cooler in summer than inland ones. The disclosure form asks directly about basement leakage and roof, wall and foundation defects, so expect buyers to start there.

Before taking any offer, list what an inspector would flag and estimate each repair. A long list favors a buyer who takes the property as-is over a retail listing that may stall on repair credits.

sections.h2: What belongs in a side-by-side check of Chicago offers?
sections.html:
Put every offer on the same footing by working out what reaches your bank account after each cost. Ask each buyer for a written offer, a proposed closing date and a statement of who pays each closing item.

  • Which party covers each city transfer tax portion, and whether the contract changes the usual split.
  • Whether the buyer closes with the building in its current condition, including any open city violations.
  • How tenants in a multi-unit building are treated, and what the leases say.
  • What happens to unpaid property tax installments and water or utility balances at closing.
  • Whether the buyer can close without a mortgage contingency or appraisal.

Get a second offer or a listing opinion from a local broker for comparison.

faqs.q: How fast can a house sell in Chicago?
faqs.a: Speed depends on title work, tenants and how quickly the transfer declaration and deed are filed. A purchase by a cash buyer skips the loan and appraisal steps that a financed purchase adds.

faqs.q: Who pays the Chicago transfer tax?
faqs.a: The Department of Finance says the buyer generally pays $3.75 per $500 and the seller $1.50 per $500 of the transfer price. The state tax is separate, and your contract can assign each piece differently, so confirm the split with your title company.

faqs.q: Do I need to repair my Chicago house before selling?
faqs.a: No. Illinois allows an as-is sale, but you still must complete and deliver the residential disclosure report before the buyer signs. Repairs help a retail sale, while an as-is buyer prices the work into the offer.

faqs.q: Where does the deed get filed after a Chicago closing?
faqs.a: The Cook County Clerk's Recordings Division handles it. The title company or attorney usually files the deed together with the declaration made online through MyDec.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Chicago house that has tenants in it?
faqs.a: Yes. Give the buyer copies of the leases and rent records, and ask your attorney how the leases and any deposits should be handled at closing.
